summary: Driftwatch is an offline-first early-warning health copilot for astronauts on long missions. It learns each astronaut’s own baseline and flags drift in radiation exposure, sleep and mood strain, bone and muscle health, cabin CO2, and nutrition. Every alert is explainable: it gives the reason, a suggested action, how to measure, and a source. A clickable body map shows Normal, Watch or Act with words as well as colour, and serious alerts say when to contact the flight surgeon. It runs entirely in the browser with no network, and builds a one-page ground report for when the link to Earth opens. It is decision support, not a medical device, and all demo data is simulated.
details:
What is the purpose of your project?

To help astronauts assess their own health during long missions, when help from Earth is delayed and they carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves. Driftwatch gathers simple health indicators, compares them with each person’s own baseline and NASA limits, and tells the astronaut what to do next.

What problem does your solution solve?

Space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity and a closed environment can cause slow, easy-to-miss changes: bone and muscle loss, poor sleep and strain, rising CO2, early signs of infection. A single reading rarely looks alarming, so problems are noticed late. Driftwatch watches trends, combines signals (for example temperature up with sleep down), and raises early, plain-language alerts. It also works with the network off and produces a ground report for the flight surgeon when the link opens.

Why is your work important?

Missions to the Moon and Mars will be longer and further from Earth. Crews will need tools that support autonomous health decisions, explain their reasoning, and never hide behind a colour. Driftwatch shows how a small, offline, transparent tool can give early warnings across several hazards at once, and labels every limit as a NASA source or our own design value, so nobody mistakes it for medical advice.

How did you use AI? (code, images, video)

We used AI assistants (Kiro and Claude) to help plan the project, write specifications, generate and review code, write tests, and draft documentation. Our team reviewed, tested and edited the output. Teammates wrote the Radiation, Isolation and BMD and strength modules; AI helped integrate and wrap them. We did not use AI to generate images or video. [If you did, add: AI-generated images or video in the demo are labelled as AI-generated.] All health data in the demo is simulated. Details are in AI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repository.

Technologies and how they were used

React + Vite (JavaScript): the app’s screens, which are the dashboard, body map, region detail, check-in, ground report, Sources page, and the in-app BMD and strength screen.

Tailwind CSS: all the styling, with a dark “Mission control” theme and colour tokens kept in one place.

Dexie (IndexedDB): saves readings on the device, so nothing goes to a server and the app works offline.

vite-plugin-pwa (service worker): makes it an installable offline web app. The build lists the files it caches, including the BMD tracker files.

Vitest, fast-check, fake-indexeddb: the tests, which cover the engine, rules, scenario, store, UI behaviour and property-based checks. Your last full run had 1,000+ tests passing.

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS: the BMD and strength tracker, written by a teammate (graphs, tooltips, weekly checklist) and embedded in the app.

Chart library: used for the trend charts. The plan said Chart.js, so check package.json for what Kiro actually installed.

Git and GitHub: version control and teamwork.

Kiro and Claude: AI assistants for planning, specs, code, tests and documents.
